newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Jubilant Taiwan welcome for Chinese "goddess".
newsitem.headline: Jubilant Taiwan welcome for Chinese "goddess".

text.p: A statue of the goddess Matsu arrived from China on Friday for a tour of Taiwan as worshippers jammed the airport and state television interrupted programmes for live coverage.

Considered by many to be the goddess herself, the life-size, gold-plated Matsu bedecked in jewellery was greeted with a drum-beating welcome from 2,000 idolaters in the biggest recent cultural exchange between political rivals Taiwan and China.
Apart from protests by a small pro-independence party, the island's people appeared jubilant at seeing one of their most beloved deities "in person" for the first time.
"Matsu will protect me from all harm," exclaimed one elderly woman on state-funded Taiwan Television, which interrupted its noon newscast to air the arrival live.
"I have been waiting for her to come all my life," a man said.
Matsu has been worshipped by Chinese for centuries, her legend passed through the generations as folklore.
The most common version is of a girl who became a guardian to seafarers after she failed to save her father from drowning in choppy waters off China's southeastern coast.
The statue that arrived on Friday came from Matsu's home shrine in Meizhou, an island off China's southeastern coast. It will tour major temples across the island for 100 days.
Reporters who accompanied the statue by plane said Matsu sat in the first-class cabin and was offered food and drink by flight attendants.

Sponsoring temples said it was the first time that Matsu had visited Taiwan, which split with China in 1949 at the end of their civil war but still has close cultural ties with the mainland and shares much common culture.
The statue was not without detractors in Taiwan, however.

About 200 members of the Taiwan Independence Party, which advocates the island's independence from China, waved banners at the airport reading: "Chinese people should worship Chinese gods, Taiwanese people should worship Taiwanese gods."
The independence party had denounced the statue's arrival as a ploy by Beijing to ensure Taiwan is brought under its eventual rule through cultural infiltration.
